title: The periodontium
blurb: The gum, ligament, cementum and bone that hold each tooth in its socket, and what happens when they break down.
question: A patient is puzzled. The dentist mentioned 'bone loss' on their radiographs, yet their teeth look fine, and one lower tooth now feels slightly loose. Which tissues hold a tooth firmly in its socket, and which of them has been lost?

teach.body: Periodontium means 'around the tooth'. It is the group of four tissues that attach each tooth to the jaw and protect that attachment: the gingiva (gum), the periodontal ligament (PDL), the cementum covering the root, and the alveolar bone that forms the socket. Cementum belongs to both camps: it is a tooth tissue and a supporting tissue. Whenever you hear 'periodontal disease', these are the tissues being damaged.

teach.h: Where the four supporting tissues sit
teach.caption: The gingiva cuffs the neck of the tooth. Below it, the thin PDL fills the gap between the root's cementum and the bony socket wall.

teach.h: The four tissues and their jobs
head: Tissue
What it is
Main job
rows: Thin hard layer on the root

teach.body: Healthy gum is coral pink (it can be naturally darker in people with more pigmented skin), firm, stippled like orange peel, with a thin knife-edge margin. The free (marginal) gingiva forms a cuff round the tooth with a shallow groove inside it, the gingival sulcus or crevice. The attached gingiva is bound firmly to the bone, and the interdental papilla fills the gap between teeth. At the base of the sulcus, the junctional epithelium attaches to the tooth and seals the body off from the mouth.

items.label: Healthy attached gingiva
items.sub: Coral pink, firm, stippled, does not bleed

items.label: Gingivitis
items.sub: Red, swollen, shiny, bleeds on brushing or probing

items.label: Alveolar mucosa
items.sub: Naturally redder, thin and movable, below the attached gum

teach.caption: The line where firm attached gingiva meets the looser alveolar mucosa is the mucogingival junction.

teach.h: The PDL: a hammock, not glue
teach.body: A tooth is not fused to the bone. It is slung in its socket by the periodontal ligament, a very thin layer of fibrous connective tissue made mostly of collagen fibres. The fibre ends (Sharpey's fibres) are embedded in cementum on one side and alveolar bone on the other. When you bite, the fibres take the strain and the tooth gives very slightly, then springs back. The PDL also carries blood vessels and nerve endings that sense pressure, so you can tell how hard you are biting.

letters.sub: Holds the tooth in its socket
Blood vessels feed cementum and bone
Tells you how hard you are biting
Its cells remodel cementum and bone, so teeth can move (orthodontics)

teach.body: The alveolar process is the part of the maxilla and mandible that holds the tooth sockets. It exists to support teeth: after an extraction the empty socket heals and the ridge gradually shrinks. On a radiograph the socket wall shows as a thin white line (the lamina dura) with the PDL as a thin dark line just inside it. In periodontitis, bacteria and the body's inflammatory response destroy the PDL and alveolar bone, which shows on radiographs as bone loss and in the mouth as pockets and loosening teeth.

teach.h: Gum disease: which tissues are hit?
teach.caption: OH = oral hygiene. You will meet both diseases in detail in Oral Disease.

teach.text: The tissue that actually ANCHORS the tooth is the periodontal ligament. Alveolar bone forms the socket and cementum gives the fibres a grip, but the PDL fibres are the 'ropes' joining the two. Gingivitis inflames the GINGIVA only; bone is not lost until periodontitis.

items: Periodontium = gingiva, periodontal ligament, cementum and alveolar bone.
Healthy gingiva: coral pink, firm, stippled, knife-edge margin, no bleeding.
PDL: fibrous connective tissue joining root cementum to alveolar bone; anchors the tooth and acts as a shock absorber.
Alveolar bone forms the sockets; it is destroyed in periodontitis and shows as bone loss on radiographs.

summary: You can now name the four tissues of the periodontium, describe healthy gingiva, explain how the periodontal ligament anchors and cushions a tooth, and say which tissues are affected in gingivitis compared with periodontitis.

A.q: A dentist is explaining the periodontium to a new trainee. Which of these is NOT part of the periodontium?
A.why: The periodontium is the gingiva, periodontal ligament, cementum and alveolar bone. Dentine is a tooth tissue beneath the enamel and cementum.

whyNot.0: The gingiva seals the neck of the tooth and is one of the four supporting tissues.
whyNot.1: Cementum covers the root and anchors the PDL fibres, so it counts as part of the periodontium.
whyNot.3: Alveolar bone forms the socket and is part of the periodontium.

A.q: A patient bites hard on a boiled sweet and feels the tooth give very slightly before settling back. Which structure is mainly absorbing that force?
A.why: The collagen fibres of the PDL take the strain of biting, letting the tooth move slightly and spring back, like a shock absorber.

whyNot.0: Enamel and dentine are rigid tooth tissues; they transmit force rather than cushion it.
whyNot.2: The gingival margin is soft tissue at the neck; it does not suspend the tooth.
whyNot.3: Pulp nerves register pain; the pulp plays no part in cushioning biting forces.

A.q: A radiograph shows a reduced level of supporting bone around several teeth. Which disease is this most consistent with?
A.why: Periodontitis destroys the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone, which shows on radiographs as bone loss.

whyNot.0: Gingivitis affects the gum only and causes no bone loss.
whyNot.1: Enamel caries affects the tooth crown, not the supporting bone.
whyNot.2: Pulpitis is inflammation of the pulp inside the tooth, not loss of supporting bone.

B.q: Which statement correctly describes the periodontal ligament?
B.why: The PDL is fibrous connective tissue, mainly collagen fibres, with blood vessels, nerves and cells.

whyNot.1: Cementum and bone are mineralised; the PDL is soft connective tissue between them.
whyNot.2: Keratinised gum describes the attached gingiva, not the ligament.
whyNot.3: Enamel covers only the crown and contains no fibres.

B.q: During a check-up the dentist records that a patient's gums are red, swollen and bleed on probing, with no bone loss. Which tissue is inflamed?
B.why: Red, swollen gums that bleed, with no bone loss, describe gingivitis: inflammation of the gingiva only.

whyNot.0: No bone loss is present, so the alveolar bone is not affected.
whyNot.1: PDL destruction happens in periodontitis and would show attachment and bone loss.
whyNot.2: Cementum lies on the root below the gum and is not what looks red and swollen.

B.q: What anchors the periodontal ligament fibres at each end?
B.why: The fibre ends (Sharpey's fibres) are embedded in cementum on the root and in the alveolar bone of the socket.

whyNot.0: Enamel is on the crown, above the ligament, and the gingiva is soft tissue.
whyNot.2: Dentine and pulp are inside the tooth; PDL fibres don't reach them.
whyNot.3: Both are soft tissues and cannot anchor the fibres that hold the tooth.

C.q: A nurse describes healthy gingiva to a patient. Which description is correct?
options: Shiny red with a rolled margin
C.why: Healthy attached gingiva is coral pink (or naturally pigmented), firm, stippled, with a knife-edge margin that doesn't bleed.

whyNot.0: Shiny red gum with a rolled margin is a sign of gingivitis.
whyNot.2: A bluish, spongy gum suggests inflammation or congestion, not health.
whyNot.3: Healthy attached gingiva is bound firmly to bone, not loose, and is pink rather than white.

C.q: Which part of the jaw forms the tooth sockets and is gradually lost after teeth are extracted?
C.why: The alveolar process holds the sockets. It exists to support teeth, so the ridge shrinks once teeth are lost.

whyNot.0: Basal bone is the main body of the jaw below the alveolar process and doesn't form sockets.
whyNot.1: The condylar process forms part of the jaw joint (TMJ).
whyNot.3: The coronoid process is where the temporalis muscle attaches, not where teeth sit.

C.q: Apart from anchoring the tooth, which is a function of the periodontal ligament?
C.why: Nerve endings in the PDL sense pressure, so you can judge how hard you are biting.

whyNot.0: Saliva is produced by the salivary glands.
whyNot.1: Enamel can't be formed after eruption because the ameloblasts are lost.
whyNot.3: Taste is detected by taste buds, mainly on the tongue.

reteach.title: Think of a tooth as a tent pole
reteach.question: Picture a tent pole standing in the ground, held up by guy ropes. What plays the part of the ground, the ropes, the pegs and the weatherproof flap at the bottom?

blocks.body: The root is the pole. The alveolar bone is the ground it stands in. The periodontal ligament is the set of guy ropes, and cementum is the coating on the pole that the ropes are tied into. The gingiva is the weatherproof flap sealed round the base, stopping dirt getting down beside the pole. If the flap gets inflamed, that's gingivitis. If the ropes rot and the ground washes away, that's periodontitis, and the pole starts to wobble.

blocks.caption: In periodontitis the bone level drops, a true pocket forms and the tooth loses support.

blocks.h: How biting force reaches the jaw

explain.body: The periodontium is the gingiva, periodontal ligament, cementum and alveolar bone. Together they hold the tooth in the jaw and protect that attachment. Enamel, dentine and pulp are tooth tissues, not supporting tissues.

test.q: Which group lists only tissues of the periodontium?
test.why: These four tissues together make up the periodontium.

whyNot.0: Enamel, dentine and pulp are tooth tissues, not supporting tissues.
whyNot.2: Pulp and enamel are part of the tooth itself.
whyNot.3: Dentine is a tooth tissue; cementum is the missing supporting tissue.

explain.body: Healthy gum is coral pink, firm and stippled with a knife-edge margin. It forms a shallow sulcus round the tooth, sealed at its base by the junctional epithelium. Gingivitis is inflammation of this tissue only: red, swollen and bleeding, but reversible.

test.q: What is the shallow groove between the free gingiva and the tooth called?
test.why: The gingival sulcus (crevice) is the normal shallow groove between the free gingiva and the tooth.

whyNot.0: A periodontal pocket is a diseased, deepened sulcus with loss of attachment.
whyNot.1: The mucogingival junction is where attached gingiva meets alveolar mucosa.
whyNot.2: The interdental papilla is the gum filling the space between two teeth.

explain.body: A thin layer of fibrous connective tissue, mostly collagen. Its fibres are embedded in cementum and alveolar bone, slinging the tooth in its socket. It supports, nourishes, absorbs shock, senses pressure and remodels the surrounding tissues.

test.q: Which structure is mainly responsible for anchoring a tooth within its socket?
test.why: The PDL fibres join the root cementum to the alveolar bone, anchoring the tooth.

whyNot.1: The junctional epithelium seals the gum to the tooth; it doesn't hold the tooth in.
whyNot.2: The attached gingiva is bound to bone but doesn't suspend the tooth.
whyNot.3: Enamel covers the crown and has no role in attachment.

explain.body: The tooth-bearing part of the maxilla and mandible. It forms the socket and is remodelled throughout life. Periodontitis destroys it, which shows as bone loss on radiographs. After extraction the ridge gradually shrinks.

test.q: A patient with periodontitis shows destruction of the bone around the roots. Which structure has been lost?
test.why: Periodontitis destroys the alveolar bone that forms and supports the sockets.

whyNot.0: Basal bone is the main body of the jaw below the tooth-bearing alveolar process.
whyNot.2: Dentine is a tooth tissue, not supporting bone.
whyNot.3: The hard palate is the bony roof of the mouth, not tooth-supporting bone.
